author: Claude (English teacher role)
basis: Shape: two sentences of 16-20 words per slide. The level is structural, not just lexical: concession, passive and participle clauses throughout, clefts on slides 5 and 17, a fronted inversion on slide 7 ("Only when help is easy to find will it reach the household..."), and reduced relatives on slides 12, 16 and 19. Kept conversational - it is a spoken talk, not an essay. Every slide rewritten at all three levels against the v2 quality gate and the grammatical-range check. The workbook text passed on averages only: its A2 averaged FK 6.9 with 12 of 20 slides over the 20-second clock, and its A2 and B1 were largely the same sentences with harder words swapped in. Level is carried by syntax and lexical load, not by word count. Facts, order and every named item of the source are kept. Corrections, none silent: (1) slide 6 - the source's "poverty becomes less visible, but more powerful" is overstated; digital exclusion makes poverty harder to see, and nothing supports the claim that it makes poverty stronger, so only the visibility claim survives. (2) slide 15 - "floods, heat and extreme weather hurt low-income families first" is wrong about timing, because a flood reaches every house in its path at the same moment; the defensible claim, and the one the source means, is that low-income families are hurt hardest, lose more and recover more slowly. (3) slide 2 - "poverty is a system problem, not only a personal failure" hedges against its own point; rewritten as a fault in the system rather than a personal failure. (4) slide 20 - the source opens the closing slide with "Thank you for listening"; the house rule is to end on the claim, so the thanks is dropped and the slide ends on the claim. The workbook's "let us" (slides 1 and 20) becomes "let's". (5) slide 7 - the source's "health insurance" is named as Taiwan's National Health Insurance at B2, a precision rather than a new fact; A2 carries three of the four safety nets (social help, health insurance, emergency money) because of the clock, while B1 and B2 carry all four including local service centers. (6) slide 12 - "this improves English" is a claim about learning outcomes, so it is hedged to "tends to improve" at B2. (7) slides 11 and 13 - "elderly care" and "old people" are rendered as "older people", which slide 16 on dignity requires. Two source generalisations are kept but left hedged rather than sharpened, because neither carries evidence: that community groups find needs official systems miss (slide 9), and that financial literacy leads to safer choices (slide 10, where the source's own "education cannot replace fair wages" is kept).

slides.1: Prosperity is remarkably good at hiding hardship, which is why my first question is uncomfortable. Does poverty still exist in a developed Taiwan, or have we simply been trained not to notice it?
slides.2: Ending poverty in all of its forms is the first global goal, and that wording deliberately reaches past household income. It covers housing, protection and access, so poverty is framed as a structural condition rather than a personal fault.
slides.3: Excellent universities, health coverage for all and a world-class chip industry have not abolished inequality here. Behind an ordinary front door there may be debt, a relative who needs daily care, or a contract that expires next month.
slides.4: Working poverty unsettles us because it breaks the promise that effort brings security. Parents trapped in temporary contracts give up the attention their children need, and the disadvantage is passed on, quietly, to the next generation.
slides.5: What an unaffordable rent removes is not simply money but everything that money would otherwise have purchased. Teenagers who relocate annually, or study on a bunk bed, reach school short of sleep, concentration and self-belief.
slides.6: Digital participation has become a precondition for opportunity rather than a convenience. A student without a working device, a stable connection and help at home is shut out of homework, research and artificial intelligence.
slides.7: Taiwan's protective net is genuinely broad: National Health Insurance, social welfare, emergency relief and local service centers. Only when help is easy to find will it reach the household that needs it before the crisis arrives.
slides.8: Schools matter enormously because they see students every single day, which no welfare office could manage. Free meals, scholarships, counseling and supervised study take real weight off a household, and an alert teacher becomes the bridge to community help.
slides.9: Civil society reaches the households that the official system overlooks, providing food, tutoring, daily care and job information. SDG 1, however, is not an argument for charity, because the aim is capability and dignity rather than dependence.
slides.10: Financial literacy offers a modest but real form of personal power, covering budgets, savings, debt, insurance and the recognition of fraud. It cannot substitute for a decent wage, though it does tend to strengthen resilience against a sudden shock.
slides.11: Careful analysis can expose the hardship that an average hides, letting students map where services, transport and after-school help run out. Communities can then aim their money well, provided we remember that each data point is a real person.
slides.12: Service learning turns an abstract target into something actually done: interviews with social workers, guides written in two languages, hours in a tutoring program. English tends to improve under those conditions, because the language finally serves a real purpose.
slides.13: Demographic change is moving poverty risk onto the oldest: anyone living alone, managing a chronic illness, or stranded when the counter became an app. The goal therefore reaches into pensions, buses, clinics and neighborly contact, not wages alone.
slides.14: For migrant workers and new immigrant families, entitlement and access are split by language, paperwork and official habit. Help that cannot be understood is help that does not exist, so inclusion has to be clear, multilingual and respectful.
slides.15: Climate change acts as an inequality multiplier, because the same flood hits two homes very differently, depending on savings and insurance. Adaptation is poverty policy, and shelters, advice and local networks must exist before the emergency arrives.
slides.16: Dignity deserves treatment as a design principle rather than a courtesy, since help delivered with contempt is often refused. People in poverty are disadvantaged rather than lacking, and support built with them works better than support built for them.
slides.17: The overall position is encouraging although nothing like sufficient, because the institutions exist and the coverage is broad. What is still missing is access, timing and the fairness with which help actually reaches the households that need it.
slides.18: Perhaps the most powerful reform is a change of vocabulary, since the word lazy closes an argument that evidence should open. Replace it with a question about obstacles, and suddenly you are debating pay, rent, clinics, buses and schools.
slides.19: Students often underestimate their own power: bilingual campaigns, volunteer work, stories, simple tools, a talk given in front of a real audience. PechaKucha turns private study into public argument, which is exactly what a democracy needs.
slides.20: Eliminating poverty sounds impossibly large, yet every credible version begins locally, by noticing a need, checking the facts, speaking with respect and working with other people. A fair future begins with whatever this generation decides is worth noticing today.
